claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an FCC matrix.
The additive-manufacturing process produces inherent microstructural heterogeneities in this alloy.
Increasing oxygen partial pressure accelerates oxygen diffusion in the alloy or its oxide scale.
Rapid oxygen transport produces a thick and heterogeneous oxide scale.
The oxide formed at high oxygen partial pressure is brittle.
Accumulated oxide growth stresses and interfacial defects promote oxide-scale spallation.
Limited oxygen availability under reducing conditions produces a thinner, more uniform, and more adherent oxide scale.
A thin, continuous, adherent oxide scale inhibits oxygen ingress and metal-cation transport and therefore improves oxidation resistance.
An oxide scale that accumulates stress more slowly and accommodates stress through deformation or defect healing has greater resistance to spallation.
Loss of protective oxide-scale integrity governs degradation and can lead to catastrophic failure.
Gas composition modulates oxide thickness, continuity, adhesion, and growth-stress development.
Pure-oxygen exposure will cause more rapid and heterogeneous oxide growth, spallation, and crack initiation than lower-oxygen or reducing exposure.
Reducing exposure will delay crack propagation relative to high-oxygen exposure.
A crossover in degradation behavior will occur as oxygen partial pressure is varied.
High-oxygen samples will exhibit a measurable increase in oxide growth stress before spallation relative to samples under reducing conditions.
The proposed behavior applies near 800 degrees Celsius over atmospheres ranging from pure oxygen to approximately 5–10% oxygen.
Intrinsic microstructural heterogeneities and residual stresses may contribute to the oxidation behavior.
The cited observations at 900–1000 degrees Celsius on other alloy variants are applicable to this additively manufactured HEA at approximately 800 degrees Celsius.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis labels 5–10% O2 balanced with either H2 or N2 as reducing conditions. Dilution with N2 creates a lower-oxygen oxidizing atmosphere rather than a reducing one, while an O2/H2 mixture cannot be classified as reducing without specifying the resulting equilibrium oxygen potential or H2/H2O ratio.

The intervention specifies cycling individual exposures between atmospheres, whereas the falsification design specifies parallel tests under separate atmospheres. These protocols probe different effects because cycling introduces transient and thermal/chemical-history contributions.

The design proposes continuous monitoring of oxide-scale characteristics using cross-sectional SEM, but conventional cross-sectional SEM or TEM is destructive and cannot continuously monitor the same specimen during exposure.
